subject: CFB58B5793CB4B10BCCDDE3EC1B51C19
introduction: This guide gathers the Bahá’í writings’ statements that the Word of God has no equal: that it is above sound and letter, that its meaning and not its recitation is the point, that no assembly of men and jinn could produce its like, and, in sentence after sentence, that a single letter of it outweighs every book and every treasure. The Qur’an is the source of the challenge, and its verses are here: produce a surah like it; if the sea were ink; if the trees were pens. The Bible speaks the same praise in other images: sweeter than honey, more than gold, a sword, a lamp, a word that stands when the grass withers; and Elijah’s still small voice says how unlike noise it is. The companions that pull the other way are honest ones. Carlyle could not find the excellence in translation; Paine doubts that any text proves its source; Socrates says inspired poets are inimitable too; Milton speaks for the worth of human books; Tertullian shows where “what has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” leads; and Pilate’s question hangs unanswered.
questions: Reading 4 says the scriptures are read only to grasp their meaning; the later readings praise the Word beyond all comparison. How does the first claim govern the second?
Carlyle found the Qur’an toilsome. If the Word’s incomparability is not evident to every reader, to whom is the challenge “produce the like” addressed, and what kind of proof is it?
Socrates says poets do not make their poems by art. How would you distinguish the inimitability claimed for revelation from that of great poetry?
Milton calls a good book “the precious life-blood of a master spirit”. Can one hold reading 37 and still prize human books? How?
“What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” What separates reading 83 from Tertullian’s rejection of philosophy?

outside.why: The Word of God “is higher and far superior to that which the senses can perceive”. Elijah on the mountain: the Lord was not in the wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire; and after the fire a still small voice.
It is sanctified above sound and letter. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
No comfort is greater than the light of the Words of God. Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart.
“What is truth? Truth is the word of God.” Jesus prays: sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.

The question the reading asks is Pilate’s, and in the Gospel it goes unanswered: Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? and went out. What would it take for the reading’s answer to reach a man in Pilate’s position?
It “gives life to humanity”. The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
Scriptures are read “for no other purpose” than to grasp their meaning. Understandest thou what thou readest?
Luke says the risen Jesus did for his friends what the reading asks of every reader: then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.
Reading without that purpose profits nothing. The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
The Word as nourishment. Man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord.
Blessed is whoever finds the fragrance of inner meanings. How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth.
The Word is “collective wisdom, absolute knowledge”. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
“Doth not that Book suffice you?” The reading echoes the Qur’an: is it not enough for them that We have sent down unto thee the Scripture which is read unto them?
The reading cites the challenge: though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur’an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another.

Carlyle, who admired Muhammad, found the Qur’an in translation as toilsome reading as he ever undertook, a wearisome confused jumble, and yet granted that a book which has moved so many must have something in it. What does the claim of inimitability mean for a reader to whom the excellence does not appear?
“A single verse … sufficeth as proof.” If ye are in doubt concerning that which We reveal unto Our slave, then produce a surah of the like thereof.
No one could produce the like of this Book. The officers’ report of Jesus is a judgment of the same kind, made on hearing: never man spake like this man.
One verse equals in decree the verses of the Prophets. He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
“Can any besides God reveal a single verse?” The Qur’an offers a test: will they not then ponder on the Qur’an? If it had been from other than God they would have found therein much incongruity.
Paine: it is revelation to the first person only, and hearsay to every other. An inimitable text is offered as the proof that travels. Does a quality of writing prove a source?
A hundred thousand verses. The Qur’an: though the sea became ink for the words of my Lord, verily the sea would be used up before the words of my Lord were exhausted.

Men cannot produce its like. Socrates says great poetry is not produced by art at all but by a divine power moving the poet, as the magnet moves iron. If inimitability marks inspiration, what distinguishes scripture from the poetry Socrates describes?
Those present when the verses surged could not bear them. The Qur’an: if We had caused this Qur’an to descend upon a mountain, thou verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of God.
Verses beyond every enumerator’s reckoning. If all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, were ink, the words of God could not be exhausted.
John ends his Gospel with the same hyperbole: I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written.
The Writings “cannot be translated” so as to be like the original. The translator of Sirach: the same things uttered in Hebrew, and translated into another tongue, have not the same force in them.
The lower cannot comprehend what is above it. As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
No breeze compares with the breezes of Revelation. The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.
A single word “cannot be equaled by all the books of the world”. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

Milton calls a good book the precious life-blood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up to a life beyond life. He speaks for all the books that the reading sets below a single word. What is a reader to do with Homer, Plato and Shakespeare after reading this?
A single letter more precious than heaven and earth. More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold.
The Word is the first cause of universal gathering. At Pentecost every nation under heaven hears the same speech.
The entire world cannot equal a single word. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
“All books are but a letter of this Book.” Jesus claimed to fulfil the law and the prophets, not to dwarf them. What attitude toward earlier scriptures do readings 56 to 62 leave the believer with?

The books of the world “have submitted”. Deuteronomy: ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it. Every scripture that claims to complete an earlier one meets this sentence. How do the readings understand it?
All that kings have in their coffers cannot compare. The kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; for joy thereof a man selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
Pearls and all that lies in the mines cannot compare. Where shall wisdom be found? Man knoweth not the price thereof; it cannot be gotten for gold.
Be grateful to have been mentioned by the Beloved. I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.

One Tablet “is more comprehensive than fifty volumes of the world’s greatest wisdom”. Sir Thomas Browne read divinity in two books, the written one of God and the universal manuscript of nature, open to all. Is the second book also set beneath the first?

The Cause “will overpower all the science, philosophy, and metaphysics of this Day”. Tertullian said it for the Church: what has Athens to do with Jerusalem? Elsewhere the Bahá’í writings insist on the harmony of religion and science. How should this sentence be read beside them?
A word God utters, however commonplace, is invested with supreme power. By the word of the Lord were the heavens made.

shortfall: Some fifty of the readings (37 to 81) repeat a single comparison in closely similar words, that all the books or treasures of the world do not equal one word or letter of God’s; companions were given to the comparison and its forms, not to each.
